text.en: Find the notes of line 1: each one waits until you're on it.
Mendelssohn wrote this tune in 1840 for a festival song marking 400 years since the printing press, not for Christmas at all.
Hear line 1, then sing it back.
Hear line 2, then sing it back.
Line 3 is the tune of line 1 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Now lines 1 to 3 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Hear line 4, then sing it back.
Hear line 5, then sing it back.
Line 6 is the tune of line 5 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Now lines 4 to 6 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Hear line 7, then sing it back.
Hear line 8, then sing it back.
Now lines 7 and 8 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Hear line 9, then sing it back.
Hear line 10, then sing it back.
Now lines 9 and 10 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Verse 1 start to end, with the guide.
Refrain start to end, with the guide.
The whole song, with the guide.
Sing your part with the other parts, and the guide with you. Hold your line while the others move.
The guide drops out: your part with the others only. Give me my note plays your first note quietly.
Once more on your own, from the top.
Record the tune of Hark! The Herald Angels Sing in Sing, with the other parts playing.
An organist at Waltham Abbey, William Hayman Cummings, fitted Mendelssohn's music to Charles Wesley's words in the 1850s, and the pairing stuck.
